name: Polysilicone-15
lead: Polysilicone-15 (dimethicodiethylbenzalmalonate; trade name Parsol SLX, from DSM) is a siloxane-based oligomer used as a UVB filter, with peak absorption near 310 nm.[1] It is a colourless to pale-yellow liquid, practically insoluble in water.[1] It is approved for sunscreens and cosmetics in the EU, and appears in hair products such as shampoos, sprays and colour treatments.[1] It also appears in US-listed lip-balm sunscreens combined with other filters.[2]

An in vitro study of 18 EU-authorised filters examined how filter concentration affects measured SPF.[3] Case reports describe allergic contact reactions to polysilicone-15 in a lip balm and in a sunscreen cream.[4][5]

paras: It is used in sunscreens, lip balms and hair-care products to absorb UVB.[1][2] A US-listed sunscreen lip balm combines it with ethylhexyl methoxycinnamate, homosalate, octocrylene and butyl methoxydibenzoylmethane, with label claims of helping prevent sunburn when used with other sun-protection measures.[2]

Allergic contact cheilitis from polysilicone-15 in a lip-care balm was reported in 2014, and allergic contact dermatitis involving polysilicone-15 and another filter (Tinosorb S) in a sunscreen cream was reported in 2022.[4][5] Wikipedia contains no further safety data.[1]
No controlled clinical trials found. Evidence consists of an in vitro SPF study covering 18 EU-authorised filters and individual case reports of contact allergy.[3][4][5]

card.summary: A silicone-polymer UVB filter (Parsol SLX) used in sunscreens, lip balms and hair products, with only case-report safety data.
card.note: Case reports describe contact allergy; no clinical trials found.

quick.overview:
Polysilicone-15 is a large silicone-based UVB filter sold as Parsol SLX. It is used in sunscreens, lip balms and some hair products.

An in vitro study covered it among 18 EU filters, and published safety data are limited to a few case reports.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVB light with a maximum near 310 nm; its polymer-like size is intended to keep it on the skin's surface.
quick.risks: Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis and cheilitis. No controlled clinical trials are documented.
